newsitem.title: USA: Mass. businesses weigh in on utility restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Mass. businesses weigh in on utility restructuring.

text.p: Massachusetts business, consumer and environmental groups united on Tuesday against proposed legislation which would give electric utilties full recovery of stranded assets in a competitive market.

"We should take a closer look at the stranded costs recovery guarantee," said Carolyn Boviard, Massachusetts director of the Natioal Federation of Independent Business, which has more than 10,000 members in the state.
"When small firms make adjustments as a result of regulations, and then the regs are changed, they don't have a guaranteed recovery for their past costs," she said.

The Smaller Business Association of New England, a group of 1,400 companies in the six state region, also called on the state legislature to reexamine the issue of stranded costs at a press conference at the State House.
"We're very anxious to see this opportunity to open that discussion," said Julie Scofield, executive director of the SBANE.
Both Boviard and Scofield welcomed proposals which would cut electric bills by 10 percent, but said that more savings could be realized through restructuring and passed along to small businesses.

Mass. Representative John Klimm, whose district on Cape Cod has among the highest utility rates in the country, introduced a bill on Monday which would limit the recovery of stranded assets following electric utility restructuring.
Klimm told reporters that his bill would require utilities to pay for their own stranded assets, which would be unused in a fully competitive market, which exceed a benchmark for the region.

"The consumer has been left behind thus far in the debate over electric utility restructuring," he said. "Many of my constituients, including the business sector, feel that proposals that have thus far been floated shift all of the financial burden as it relates to stranded costs on to their backs."
New England is at the forefront of electricity deregulation, where once-highly regulated utilities are now being told they have to compete for customers.
But Massachusetts has not formally approved its regulatory agency's plan to allow consumers a choice of electric supplier or, if they choose not to select a supplier, receive a 10 percent rate cut.
